questions.stem: A client with acute pulmonary edema is prescribed IV furosemide. The client has chronic kidney disease and baseline hearing impairment. Which administration concern is most important for the nurse to recognize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rapid IV administration increases the risk of ototoxicity; the nurse should use the prescribed controlled rate and monitor for tinnitus or worsening hearing.","B":"Rapid IV administration primarily increases the risk of severe hyperkalemia, so potassium replacement should be withheld until the infusion is complete.","C":"The client's hearing history is unrelated to furosemide because ototoxicity occurs only with oral therapy and is not associated with IV administration.","D":"Giving the IV dose rapidly is preferred because faster delivery lowers the risk of volume depletion and renal dysfunction while preserving the same diuretic effect."}}
questions.rationale: Furosemide labeling warns that tinnitus and reversible or irreversible hearing impairment have been associated with rapid injection, high doses, renal impairment, and other ototoxic drugs. IV administration should therefore follow the recommended controlled rate, with added vigilance in a client who already has renal and hearing risk factors.
questions.source_detail: Current labeling warns that rapid IV injection, high doses, and renal impairment increase ototoxicity risk; controlled IV administration is recommended.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease is newly prescribed lisinopril. Which laboratory monitoring is most important after initiation and during dose adjustment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Monitor serum calcium and magnesium because ACE inhibition most commonly causes clinically important hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia after initiation.","B":"Monitor serum potassium and renal function because lisinopril can cause hyperkalemia and clinically important changes in kidney function, especially in CKD.","C":"Monitor hemoglobin A1c and fasting glucose because ACE inhibition commonly causes treatment-limiting hyperglycemia during the first several weeks of therapy.","D":"Monitor bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase as the principal routine safety tests because predictable cholestatic injury is the main dose-limiting effect of lisinopril."}}
questions.rationale: Lisinopril labeling specifically advises periodic monitoring of renal function and serum potassium. Pre-existing kidney disease increases the importance of this surveillance because ACE inhibition can produce changes in renal function and hyperkalemia.
questions.source_detail: Current lisinopril labeling: monitor renal function periodically and monitor serum potassium for hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A client with a life-threatening fungal infection is receiving conventional amphotericin B and has a mildly elevated baseline creatinine. Which trend should the nurse prioritize during therapy?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A progressive rise in bilirubin with stable creatinine is the expected dose-limiting toxicity, so renal and electrolyte monitoring can remain routine.","B":"A fall in fasting glucose is the characteristic toxicity of amphotericin B and should be treated as the earliest marker of treatment intolerance.","C":"A rising creatinine with potassium or magnesium depletion is concerning for amphotericin-associated nephrotoxicity and requires close clinical review.","D":"New mild leukocytosis with unchanged renal function is the principal expected toxicity and usually determines whether amphotericin B must be discontinued."}}
questions.rationale: Conventional amphotericin B is nephrotoxic and its labeling recommends frequent renal monitoring, especially in patients with reduced renal function. Renal adverse effects include azotemia and hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia is also reported. Renal and electrolyte trends are therefore central to safe monitoring.
questions.source_detail: Labeling warns of nephrotoxicity, reduced renal function, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia and recommends frequent renal-function monitoring.

questions.stem: A client receiving central parenteral nutrition has glucose values rising from 130 to 260 mg/dL over 24 hours. The central-line site is clean and the client is afebrile. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The glucose rise does not by itself establish a catheter bloodstream infection because hyperglycemia and central-line infection require separate clinical assessment.","B":"The glucose rise can be ignored because parenteral nutrition does not cause clinically important hyperglycemia unless the client had diabetes before admission or severe illness.","C":"The central line should be removed solely because glucose has increased, since hyperglycemia is considered a direct diagnostic marker of catheter infection.","D":"Parenteral nutrition can contribute to hyperglycemia, which should be monitored and managed; central-line infection risk is addressed separately with meticulous catheter care."}}
questions.rationale: Parenteral nutrition can cause or worsen hyperglycemia because it provides substantial intravenous carbohydrate. Hyperglycemia requires monitoring and management, but it is not by itself diagnostic of a catheter-related bloodstream infection. Central venous access carries an independent infection risk that is reduced through evidence-based line care.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Parenteral Nutrition Care Pathway and Hyperglycemia Guidance
questions.source_detail: ASPEN guidance treats glycemic monitoring/management and central venous access safety as distinct components of parenteral nutrition care.

questions.stem: A client with prolonged profound neutropenia after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is cared for in a protective environment. A visitor brings fresh flowers and washed packaged fruit. Which nursing response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Do not bring fresh or dried flowers or potted plants into the protective environment; handle food according to safe-food practices and the transplant program's policy.","B":"Reject both the flowers and every form of fresh produce because national infection-control guidance prohibits all uncooked fruits and vegetables for every neutropenic client.","C":"Allow the flowers because plant restrictions apply only to immunocompetent clients, while protective-environment patients have no special environmental fungal risk.","D":"Permit both gifts without review because protective-environment precautions address airborne isolation only and do not include environmental controls for fungal exposure."}}
questions.rationale: CDC protective-environment guidance prohibits fresh or dried flowers and potted plants for HSCT patients because plants can harbor fungal organisms. This does not support a blanket national rule banning every raw fruit or vegetable for every neutropenic patient; food handling should follow evidence-based food-safety and transplant-program policy.
questions.source_detail: CDC Protective Environment recommendations prohibit fresh/dried flowers and potted plants for HSCT patients; food restrictions should follow the program's evidence-based policy.
